description: Looking for team members skilled in software development, data analysis, and visualizations.
summary: SPHEREx is mapping the entire sky in 102 bands of near-infrared light, producing an enormous collection of observations that can be difficult to explore. The Argonauts developed the SPHEREx Time Explorer, a public-facing web app that makes this data easier to investigate. Users can enter an object name or sky coordinates, choose a field of view, dates, and detectors, then browse available observations as a chronological image sequence. The app retrieves image cutouts through IRSA’s Simple Image Access service, processes and aligns them, and provides tools to compare observations, inspect target measurements, and stack images at similar wavelengths to improve signal-to-noise. By making SPHEREx observations more accessible and interactive, the tool helps researchers and the public look for changes in the sky and investigate potential moving or variable objects.
details:
The Argonauts developed SPHEREx Time Explorer, a public-facing web app for exploring how a patch of infrared sky changes over time. Users enter an object name or RA/Dec, then choose a field of view, observation dates, and detectors. The app searches NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive through its Simple Image Access service, retrieves calibrated FITS cutouts, measures target brightness and wavelength, and aligns images on a shared north-up grid. Users can play the images as a time sequence, track a target, inspect measurements and quality flags, and compare two observations.

To help reveal faint signals, the app can stack multiple frames selected by wavelength centre, tolerance, dates, and frame exclusions. It uses per-pixel variance to weight valid measurements and displays the resulting mean, estimated uncertainty, and coverage. Because detector responses and point-spread functions can differ, the app identifies and warns about stacks that mix detectors.

The project lowers the barrier to exploring a large archive and helps users investigate potential moving or variable objects; it supports discovery rather than automatically classifying objects. We considered data quality, proper motion, wavelength differences, image alignment, signal-to-noise, time smearing, and download performance.

We built the processing pipeline in Python with Flask, Astropy, NumPy, Requests, and Reproject. The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with WebGL and Canvas for image display. Docker Compose makes the app easier to run across Linux, macOS, and Windows. No specialized hardware is required.
